usage: to lower the price, to bargain
examples: Please give me a little discount.
nuance: 값 means the price or cost of something and is a slightly more everyday, spoken word than 가격. You will hear it most in markets and small shops, often with 싸다 (cheap) or 비싸다 (expensive). 값 also appears in the fixed phrase 값을 치르다, meaning to pay the price.
mistakes: Saying 값 비싸요 without 이 — say 값이 비싸요.
Confusing 값 (price) with 가격 (price); both are fine, but 값 sounds more casual.

nuance: 잔돈 is the small or loose money you carry, such as coins and small bills. It overlaps with 거스름돈, but 거스름돈 is specifically the change you get back after paying, while 잔돈 is any small money you happen to have. Cashiers often ask 잔돈 있으세요? to mean Do you have exact small change.
mistakes: Mixing up 잔돈 (small money you hold) and 거스름돈 (change handed back).
Saying 잔 돈 with a space — write it as one word 잔돈.

examples: Do you have a 10,000 won bill?
I had no bills, so I paid by card.
nuance: 지폐 means paper money, the bills in your wallet, as opposed to 동전 (coins). It is a calm, neutral word used when you talk about cash by its form. In daily speech people often just say the amount plus 짜리, like 만 원짜리, but 지폐 is handy when contrasting paper money with coins.
mistakes: Using 지폐 for coins — coins are 동전.
Forgetting 짜리 when stating a bill's value: say 오천 원짜리 지폐.

examples: I checked the amount on the receipt.
nuance: 금액 is the specific sum of money written on a bill, receipt, or screen. It is a little more formal than just saying 돈 and is the natural word at a counter, at the bank, or when paying online. You will often see 총 금액 (total amount) on receipts and checkout pages.
mistakes: Using 금액 to mean money in general — for that, use 돈.
Asking 금액 얼마예요 without 이 — say 금액이 얼마예요.

examples: Please tell me the total amount.
The total is shown on the receipt.
nuance: 합계 is the total you get after adding everything up, the bottom line on a bill or receipt. It is close to 총액 and 총 금액, and all are used at checkout. 합계 feels a bit like a written or printed word, so you see it on receipts more often than you say it out loud.
mistakes: Confusing 합계 (total) with 할인 (discount).
Saying 합 계 with a space — it is one word 합계.

examples: There is a really wide variety of products.
nuance: 상품 is the slightly more formal, store-style word for a product or item for sale, the kind of word you see on price tags, signs, and online shops. In everyday talk people often say 물건 instead, but 상품 sounds right for advertised or labeled goods. You will meet it in phrases like 인기 상품 and 할인 상품.
mistakes: Confusing 상품 (product) with 상품권 (gift certificate).
Using 상품 for a personal belonging — use 물건 for your own stuff.

english: regular customer, a place one frequents
usage: a shop one goes to regularly
examples: This is the shop I go to regularly.
I'm a regular at this cafe.
If you become a regular, they give a discount.
nuance: 단골 describes a regular relationship with a shop, restaurant, or its owner, either the loyal customer or the favorite place itself. Becoming a 단골 in Korea often means friendlier service and small discounts. The fuller form 단골손님 makes clear you mean the regular customer.
mistakes: Thinking 단골 only means the customer — it can also mean your regular shop.
Saying 단골 가게 with a wrong space inside 단골; 단골 is one word.

usage: to look at the price tag
examples: Please look at the price tag.
These clothes have no price tag.
I paid as marked on the tag.
nuance: 가격표 is the little tag or printed list that shows how much something costs. Checking the 가격표 is the safe way to know the set price before you ask. In Korea most stores have fixed prices on the 가격표, so bargaining is mainly for traditional markets.
mistakes: Confusing 가격표 (price tag) with 영수증 (receipt).
Dropping 표: 가격 means price, but the tag itself is 가격표.

english: lump-sum payment (paying in full at once)
usage: to pay in full at once
examples: Please charge it all at once.
I'll pay for this in full.
nuance: 일시불 means paying the whole amount in one charge, as opposed to 할부 (paying in installments). When you pay by card in Korea, the cashier almost always asks 일시불로 하시겠어요? and you answer 일시불이요 or 할부요. It is one of the most useful checkout words to know.
mistakes: Confusing 일시불 (pay in full) with 할부 (installments).
Forgetting 로: say 일시불로 해 주세요, not 일시불 해 주세요.

nuance: 할부 is paying for an expensive item in several monthly amounts instead of all at once. It is the natural opposite of 일시불, and the cashier may ask 몇 개월로 해 드릴까요? to mean how many months. Many cards offer 무이자 할부 (interest-free installments) for larger purchases.
mistakes: Mixing up 할부 (installments) and 할인 (discount).
Saying 할부 하다 without 로 — use 할부로 하다.

examples: How much is the shipping cost?
I want to cut the cost a little.
nuance: 비용 is the cost or expense of doing something, used with the verb 들다 (to cost), as in 비용이 들다. Unlike 값 or 가격, which are the price of an item, 비용 is the money needed for an activity, such as shipping, travel, or repairs. You will often hear 비용이 많이 들어요 for that is expensive to do.
mistakes: Using 비싸다 with 비용 — say 비용이 많이 들어요, not 비용이 비싸요.
Confusing 비용 (cost of an action) with 값 (price of an item).

examples: I got it for free, so I'm happy.
nuance: 공짜 is the casual, friendly word for something that costs nothing, a freebie. It is more colloquial than the formal 무료, which you see on signs and ads. People love to say 공짜 좋아요 (I love free stuff), and 공짜로 means for free.
mistakes: Forgetting 로: say 공짜로 받았어요, not 공짜 받았어요.
Using 공짜 in very formal writing — use 무료 there instead.

examples: Can we do a cash deal too?
I bought it cheap through a direct deal.
nuance: 거래 means a transaction or deal, any exchange of money for goods, whether at a store, a bank, or between two people. It is common in secondhand buying and selling, where 직접 거래 means meeting in person to trade. The verb form is 거래하다, to do business or make a deal.
mistakes: Confusing 거래 (a deal) with 거래처 (a business client).
Saying 거래 하다 with a space is fine, but the single verb is 거래하다.
